title: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft
description: Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv
body: Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled, uncrewed aircraft would "transform military aviation".His comments refer to the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a partnership between the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, expected to enter service by 2035.The aircraft, commonly known as Tempest, is expected to provide speed stealth, use advanced sensors and even AI to assist the human pilot when they are overwhelmed, or under extreme stress.Writing in the Telegraph, external, Sir Harv said the GCAP aircraft was "perhaps the last crewed fighter we will ever build", not because people would become less important, but because advances in technology were changing the nature of air combat.He said AI and machines would take on "the most dangerous tasks instead of humans", while stressing that technology should enhance human judgement and "not replace accountability". He added: "Uncrewed fighter jets will start flying in UK airspace next year. This is exciting and necessary in equal measure."Sir Harv also said the RAF of the future would combine Typhoons and F-35s with autonomous systems.The programme was announced in 2022 by the UK, Italy and Japan, which are jointly developing the aircraft. In July, the three countries signed a £4.6bn contract covering the next phase of its design through industry joint venture Edgewing.According to GCAP, the aircraft will be powered by advanced data processing and artificial intelligence, while also featuring enhanced stealth technology. The UK government says the project already supports 3,500 jobs and 1,000 apprenticeships.Canada was granted "observer nation" status in July, giving it privileged access to the programme without a decision-making role.In October, Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK government would "seek to progress" Germany joining GCAP. He said the partnership could also support cooperation on issues including "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".

schema.headline: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft

title: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
description: Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?So-called "job ghosting" has become a
body: Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training -  those dubbed as Neets - this week. Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time. Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview."With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications."It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances. But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this. Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says."It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting. But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.

schema.headline: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond

title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
description: Figure caption, Russian ship engulfed in flames after explosion at Libyan portByHafsa Khalil and Joe InwoodWorld news correspondentUpdated 56 minutes
body: Figure caption, Russian ship engulfed in flames after explosion at Libyan portByHafsa Khalil and Joe InwoodWorld news correspondentUpdated 56 minutes agoAn explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government. The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.Image source, Planet Labs PBCImage caption, Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the portUS-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI)."Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

schema.headline: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say

title: AI is being used to clone real people's videos
description: The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI charactersFigure caption, Watch: Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycatsByMarco Silva Is
body: The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI charactersFigure caption, Watch: Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycatsByMarco Silva Is this real or AI? It is a question increasingly asked underneath social media videos, and often difficult to tell.But there is a new trend when it comes to digital manipulation. Across social media, AI-generated characters are appearing in videos that look remarkably similar to those posted by real people.From musicians to dancers and comedians, content creators are finding their performances cloned by these characters that are designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualised.Experts call the practice "reskinning" and say it is made possible by cheap, easy-to-use AI tools. People can discover their work has been copied by seeing a video of a character making the same joke or doing the same dance, even with the same background. Sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original.Some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes, and to eventually make money. Others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. But the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen.Image source, BBC/Sophie LloydImage caption, Guitarist Sophie Lloyd (left) and "Mila Vasari""A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we've created," says Sophie Lloyd, a UK-based guitarist who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, who has spent years building a successful online presence.Lloyd says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person. The videos on the Vasari account also contain visual inconsistencies that suggest AI was used to create them, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music, and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed.The account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos. Its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify has found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content.But Lloyd is far from alone in having her content manipulated by AI.Image source, BBC/Kjetil Krogstad"I've got so many messages from other artists and creators that have had the same thing happening to them," says Kjetil Krogstad, a Norwegian content creator known for videos showing him happily dancing in a suit while carrying a cup of tea.In March, his followers alerted him to the fact that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny. The post went on to attract millions of views - outperforming Krogstad's original video - before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money."What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that's already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools," she says.Kendall sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture", in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money - be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult  content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms.And making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, Kendall says. "That's the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful, it really conforms with these conventional cultural ideals of attractiveness, success, aspiration, beauty."Image source, BBC/Grace RobertsDozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission."I cannot explain how angry I am right now," Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram. "Someone not only stole my video, but also changed me into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and this is literally my job," she said, showing the original video of herself wearing jeans, smiling and covering her ears at a drag car race next to an AI-generated version with a blonde woman in a short dress."I put the videos side by side and I could see it was my exact facial movements, how my body moved, the exact same background and even the people around me were completely copied," she told BBC Verify. "It was just me that had been altered.""I pay for the cars, I build the cars, I pay for the cameras, the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and then make money off the back of my video," she added.Her concerns are echoed by other content creators who fear these AI-generated accounts could cost them valuable exposure, followers, and potential income.American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video: "The thing that is most concerning is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they're real people."And for context, comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy," she said, adding that comedians spent a long time crafting jokes on stage and honing them into punchy lines.Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate.But legal protections are only part of the challenge. Identifying those responsible for copying the videos, and stopping them from doing it again, can also prove difficult.Stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole, says Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians. "You don't even know who's making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they're just going to create another," he says."It's not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I've seen this all over the internet."Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this.Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also "working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals".But for artists like Lloyd, the damage may already be done. "It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else - and then people don't even know it's you."

schema.headline: AI is being used to clone real people's videos

title: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz beats world number one Alexander Zverev to claim title
description: Carlos Alcaraz outplayed world number one Alexander Zverev to end his wait for a first ATP Finals title and complete a remarkable post-injury return t
body: Carlos Alcaraz outplayed world number one Alexander Zverev to end his wait for a first ATP Finals title and complete a remarkable post-injury return to the sport.A season which began with Alcaraz becoming the youngest man to complete the career Grand Slam, before he was ruled out for more than four months with a wrist issue, ended with the Spaniard holding aloft another of the sport's biggest trophies.Alcaraz, still wearing heavy strapping around his upper-left leg following his injury scare earlier in the week, collapsed to the ground in celebration after sealing a 6-2 7-6 (9-7) win in a dramatic second-set tie-break.It was a statement victory over Zverev, who took advantage of Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner's injury absences to rise to the top of the rankings and claim his first two major titles.It was a 14th successive win and a third-straight title triumph for seven-time major winner Alcaraz, who demonstrated beyond any doubt that he is back to his devastating best."Lifting this trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time, it means the world to me," the 23-year-old said."I have been through really difficult moments with myself, with my team. For me it's been an amazing week."I couldn't finish the week in a better way."The contrasting emotions of the two players were evident when Alcaraz wore a big grin after pulling off a between-the-legs lob that Zverev smashed into the net. At the other end of the court, the German threw away his racquet in disgust.While Alcaraz danced to music during a change of ends, Zverev's frustrations only grew as, after winning back one of the two breaks of serve, he received a second time violation on his way to losing serve for a third successive game.The top seed left the court after unravelling in the first set, having produced just three winners to 19 unforced errors in an inconsistent start.Alcaraz's march to the title appeared inevitable as he took control of the second set with a fourth break of serve, but Zverev restored parity in the eighth game and kept his hopes alive by forcing a tie-break.Overturning a 3-0 deficit in the tie-break, Zverev then won six straight points to arrive at three set points.However, he failed to take all of them, including one on his own serve, before Alcaraz drove in a backhand winner on his second match point. After picking himself off the floor, the Spaniard celebrated with his team in the stands after finally landing the title he had been chasing for four years.In the doubles, French debutants Theo Arribage and Albano Olivetti lifted the trophy after a comeback victory against Marcelo Arevalo and Mate Pavic.The sixth seeds recovered from losing the first set to win 3-6 7-6 (7-2) 10-6, ending the year with the most wins (59) and titles (seven) in men's doubles.

schema.headline: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz beats world number one Alexander Zverev to claim title

title: Hull City 2-0 Brighton: Keeper Konstantinos Tzolakis stars for Tigers after Greece nightmare
description: With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just coul
body: With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just could not find a way past former Olympiacos goalkeeper Tzolakis, who joined Hull in August for a reported £20m fee.He got down to make a vital block early on to deny Diego Gomez, who had slid in to meet a low cross from the left wing. It was the first of several occasions the Paraguay international would be frustrated in front of goal.Tzolakis then raced out spreadeagled to foil Georginio Rutter with an outstretched left hand - a stop that BBC Radio 5 Live pundit and former striker Clinton Morrison described as "Peter Schmeichel-esque", referring to the legendary Denmark keeper.Second-half efforts from distance by Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk were dealt with, too.Yasin Ayari went close with a thumping strike against the bar and when Brighton substitute Charalampos Kostoulas pounced on a short backpass to go through one-on-one, Tzolakis got a hand on his Greece team-mate's shot and Regan Slater was back on the goalline to head the ball to safety.Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy, a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said: "We saw again how important Tzolakis is for Hull. He had one of those days where he was always in the right place at the right time."When you are a Hull player and you see the kind of saves Tzolakis made when he spread himself and kept it out with his foot, you start thinking that it could be your day."It happens a lot in football and, on the flip side, Brighton will have been thinking, 'are we ever going to score here?'."

schema.headline: Hull City 2-0 Brighton: Keeper Konstantinos Tzolakis stars for Tigers after Greece nightmare

title: Redditch widow fears losing home as bereavement support ends
description: Widow fears losing home built by husband after support payments endFigure caption, Lauren's husband Andy died from cancer in 2024ByJames Pearson Heref
body: Widow fears losing home built by husband after support payments endFigure caption, Lauren's husband Andy died from cancer in 2024ByJames Pearson Hereford & Worcester political reporterEvery room in Lauren's family home reminds her of her late husband.A self-employed builder, Andy carried out much of the work on the property himself, helping create the house where the couple raised their four children.Now, more than two years after his death from cancer, Lauren fears she may struggle to keep it.The financial support that helped her cover mortgage payments and household bills has ended, leaving her facing uncertainty as she prepares to remortgage the property."I don't want to uproot my children," she said. "They've already been through too much the last two and a half years."Image source, LaurenImage caption, Lauren says Andy's biggest concern before he died was how the family would cope financiallyLauren, from Redditch, lost her husband in May 2024, just five months after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer at the age of 42.The family's income fell by about 80% after his death.She says bereavement support payments provided a lifeline while she adapted to life as the sole provider for her children.Now those payments have ended, she faces an uncertain future."Will I get a mortgage? I don't know," she said.Lauren said Andy had first begun suffering stomach complaints in December 2023, around the same time the family were looking into life insurance."By the time we really needed it, it was too late... he now had something that was pre-existing," she said.Although doctors initially gave Andy a prognosis of 16 months, his condition deteriorated rapidly."He died a very scared man," Lauren said. "His biggest worry was how I was going to cope financially."Image source, Jill & Simon HackImage caption, Lauren says she does not want to uproot her four children from the family homeAs well as a lump sum payment of £3,500, the government provides financial support of up to £350 a month to bereaved spouses, though it is time-limited.For recipients of Universal Credit like Lauren, the payments only last a year.Before 2017, support known as Widowed Parent's Allowance was available until children reached the age of 18, but it was replaced by Bereavement Support Payment.Lauren said the payments had helped cover mortgage costs, food and household bills after her husband's death.Without them, she says she is struggling to bridge the gap."I just can't find that money," she said. "I can't work any more hours than I'm working."She believes bereavement support should last longer, rise in line with inflation and be promoted more clearly."It feels like a secret benefit," she said.Image source, Widows FightImage caption, A petition calling for changes to bereavement support is due to be debated by MPsLauren's experience has led her to join campaign group Widows Fight, which is calling for changes to the system.Its petition, which attracted nearly 109,000 signatures, is due to be debated by MPs on Monday.Campaigners want support to better reflect the financial pressures facing bereaved families, particularly those with dependent children.For Lauren, however, the issue is less about politics than the practical reality of providing for her family while trying to preserve what her husband left behind.A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: "Losing a loved one is devastating and we understand the financial impact it can have on families."Bereavement Support Payment provides short-term financial support, with higher amounts paid for those with children."Further help with everyday living costs may be available through benefits such as Universal Credit which provide targeted, means-tested support to those in greatest need."If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action LineGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Hereford & Worcester

schema.headline: Redditch widow fears losing home as bereavement support ends

title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
description: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.A string of black and white photos shared
body: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the date ceremony date, 21 November.Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.The American singer confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia."I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret."We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.The singer, whose hits include Party in the U.S.A and Wrecking Ball, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

schema.headline: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony

title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
description: "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Ko
body: "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency. "Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating. His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong."I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.All this made even honest test takers paranoid.Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

schema.headline: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal

title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
description: A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.The Sparta II had been
body: A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said."War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.  Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

title: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page says she nearly messed up Gavin and Stacey audition
description: Joanna Page has said she nearly messed up her Gavin And Stacey audition after failing to do a Cardiff accent.The 49-year-old rose to fame after starri
body: Joanna Page has said she nearly messed up her Gavin And Stacey audition after failing to do a Cardiff accent.The 49-year-old rose to fame after starring as Stacey in the BBC comedy opposite creators James Corden and Ruth Jones.Page, from Swansea, told campmates on ITV's I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here! that she had initially read some scenes for Jones using her actual accent.She recounted that she was then asked to do it in a Cardiff accent, as that was where her character was supposed to be from, but Jones told her it sounded "awful" and to "just be you".Speaking about her preparations for the life-changing audition, she said: "I remember reading the script, Ruth and James had written it and I remember thinking, 'This is me, she is me, I can do this'."Page said she got the offer for the part in the Bafta-winning sitcom two weeks after being rejected from a West End show.She said: "I was working in a shoe shop in East Dulwich and I'd just missed out on getting the part in Dirty Dancing The Musical."And so if I'd have got that, I never, ever would have done it."Page also recalled her first impression of Mathew Horne - who played Gavin in the series - during their chemistry read and said "he seemed really cool, and I thought I'm not cool and I'm just a nerd".The hit series aired for three seasons from 2007 until 2009 followed by Christmas specials including the series finale in 2024.

title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
description: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talk
body: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures. The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change". "It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions. Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts. Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room."Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing"."This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change. The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century. Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says. But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world. The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia."[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
description: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Repr
body: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called. Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats. View the 2026 midterm election resultsSunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa. Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters. President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance. Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website. The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes. Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law. However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

title: Liverpool v Manchester United: How the players rated
description: Alisson Becker: Caught one cross and took a few goal-kicks. Made a good save to deny Bruno Fernandes in stoppage time. Had little else to do. 6Ronald
body: Alisson Becker: Caught one cross and took a few goal-kicks. Made a good save to deny Bruno Fernandes in stoppage time. Had little else to do. 6Ronald Araujo: Never really tested defensively. Made a few contributions going forward. 7Jeremy Jacquet: Went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo in the box at 0-0, although a penalty against the French defender would have been harsh. 6Virgil van Dijk: Organised the defence well. Also had a header well-saved at 0-0 and nodded another wide in the second half. 7Milos Kerkez: Always keen to drive Liverpool up the pitch. Had some nice link-ups with Rio Ngumoha. 7Dominik Szoboszlai: Fantastic driven free-kick to open the scoring. Went close a few more times with long shots and generally bossed the midfield. 8Alexis Mac Allister: Did all the simple things right and allowed others to shine around him. Forced Senne Lammens into a top save in the first half. 7Bradley Barcola: Missed a few chances to score his first league goal for Liverpool when through one-vs-one. Showed his electric pace to set up his side's third. 7Florian Wirtz: Readjusted well to net Liverpool's second and assisted their fourth. Five goals in four games for club and country now and looks close to his creative best. 8Rio Ngumoha: So direct and skilful. Scored Liverpool's third with a calm finish. Also set up their second after easily beating Diogo Dalot. Club and country have a real talent on their hands. 9Alexander Isak: Led the line well but missed some big chances. Won the free-kick that resulted in Szoboszlai's goal and led to Leny Yoro's sending off. 6Subs:Victor Munoz (on 72, Barcola): Good cameo and took his goal well, curling it into the far corner. 7Trey Nyoni (on 72, Mac Allister): Looked bright. Had a shot go just over. 6Jeremie Frimpong (on 78, Ngumoha): 5Joe Gomez (on 85, Araujo) 5Lewis Koumas (on 85, Isak) 5Subs not used: Chiesa, Mamardashvili, McConell, Tsimikas.Senne Lammens: Could he have done better with the opener? Good save to deny Mac Allister and some decent stops after that. 6Leny Yoro: Did he have to make the tackle on Isak? It was almost as though he thought about whether he should and decided the answer was yes. Given Liverpool scored from the free-kick it was a bad decision. 4Matthijs de Ligt: First Premier League start in almost 12 months in middle of a back three turned into a nightmare with the early error that led to opening goal and Yoro red card. Struggled from that moment on. 4Lisandro Martinez: Fully extended by Liverpool's attack. The least bad of the visitors' starting defence, but that isn't saying much. Exposed completely by Barcola for Liverpool's third. 5Diogo Dalot: Given a torrid time by Ngumoha, which prompted Pochettino to bring on Maguire. Tries hard but it's not enough. 5Youri Tielemans: Concerns about a midfield partnership with Mainoo emerge again. Not having the sustained impact required for a player of his experience. 4Kobbie Mainoo: Twenty-one-year-old being asked to shoulder so much responsibility in an ailing team. New midfield recruits have not helped him. 5Bryan Mbeumo: Couple of decent bursts came to nothing, then sacrificed after Yoro red card. Received consoling pat on the head from his new boss. 5Bruno Fernandes: Early free-kick just wide and shot straight at Alisson. Given the carnage at Old Trafford this season, no wonder contract talks on hold. Furious at free-kick given against him when he thought he was through. 5Patrick Dorgu: Asked to do an awful lot, initially as wing-back, then further back. Lucky Barcola fluffed his lines or his failure to keep an offside line would have been exposed. 5Matheus Cunha: Tried to keep simmering frustration in check. Not easy in a losing side with no service. Replaced at the break. 5Subs:Harry Maguire (on 22, Mbeumo): Couldn't have expected to be called on so soon. Went into middle of back three and immediately blocked an Isak effort to prevent a third goal. Tried hard. 5Joshua Zirkzee (on 46, Cunha): Pre-match rumours of a rare start proved unfounded. Replaced Cunha at half-time and asked to bring a different skillset to the number nine role. More physical but not as good and lost possession too easily. 4Mason Mount (on 65, Tielemans): Only on for a couple of minutes when attempted crossfield pass went to Liverpool player and eventually a third goal. 5Noussair Mazraoui (on 65, Dorgu): Not really sure what he was supposed to do. Tried to push forward as United's poor control brought more pressure. 4Andrey Santos (on 87, Mainoo): 5Subs not used: Heaton, Amad Diallo, Heaven, Lacey.

schema.headline: Liverpool v Manchester United: How the players rated
